english_translation: The Shona people were skilled artisans who could mold beautiful clay pots.

dialogue.shona: VaShona vaive mhizha dzaigona kuumba hari dzakanaka dzevhu.
dialogue.english: The Shona people were skilled artisans who could mold beautiful clay pots.
dialogue.literal_gloss: VaShona [people shona] • vaive [people ive] • mhizha [mhizha] • dzaigona [dzaigona] • kuumba [to / at umba] • hari [hari] • dzakanaka [dzakanaka] • dzevhu [dzevhu]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('dzakanaka')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'dzakanaka' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Talking About How Things Used to Be: The '-ai-' Past Habitual ('dzaigona')
grammar_notes.content: In this sentence, 'dzaigona' uses the past habitual/imperfect marker '-ai-'. Whenever you talk about how people used to live in historical times, or an ongoing state in the past ('used to do', 'was/were doing'), Shona combines the subject prefix with '-ai-' + the verb stem: for example, 'vaigara' ('they used to live'), 'vaitengeserana' ('they used to trade with one another'), 'yaivakwa' ('it used to be built'), and 'hwaizivikanwa' ('it was renowned/known').
grammar_notes.rule: Subject Prefix + -ai- + Verb Stem = 'used to [verb] / was [verb]-ing' (va- + -ai- + -bva = vaibva, 'they came from')

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('kuumba')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'kuumba' in this sentence. Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). Because 'ku-' verbs also behave as action nouns ('eating', 'paying', 'working'), you can attach linking prefixes directly to them: 'yekubhadhara' ('for paying'), 'pakubikwa' ('in the cooking'), and 'nekuona' ('by/with seeing').
grammar_notes.rule: ku- + Verb Stem = 'to [verb] / [verb]-ing' (ku- + -tenga = kutenga, 'to buy'; ye- + kubhadhara = yekubhadhara, 'for paying')

cultural_notes.title: Master Potters ('Kuumba Hari dzeVhu') & Ceramic Art in Shona Culture
cultural_notes.content: For centuries, Shona women artisans ('mhizha dzekuumba hari') have crafted finely burnished clay vessels ('hari dzevhu') etched with geometric chevron patterns—including 'tsaiya' for cooking sadza, 'hadyana' for relish, and 'chirongo' for keeping drinking water naturally cool.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you politely ask someone to speak softly ('taura zvinyoronyoro')?
In 'Uya kuno undibatsire', what does the prefix '-ndi-' inside 'undibatsire' mean?
active_exercises.explanation: The object prefix '-ndi-' always means 'me', placed directly before the verb stem '-batsira' (help).

active_exercises.prompt: What does 'parutivi pemugwagwa' mean in 'Rori yakamira parutivi pemugwagwa'?
options: In the middle of the intersection
Beside the road / on the side of the road
active_exercises.correct_answer: Beside the road / on the side of the road
active_exercises.explanation: 'Parutivi pe-' means 'beside / at the side of', and 'mugwagwa' is 'road'.
